currentWholeCardLiteral.prompt: К чьей святыне направляются паломники в «Кентерберийских рассказах» Джеффри Чосера?

answers.note: По рассказу Беды, Альбан укрыл у себя христианского священника, бежавшего от преследователей.
Томас Бекет, архиепископ Кентерберийский, был убит в 1170 году и причислен к лику святых в 1173-м.
Беда сообщает, что Кутберт стал епископом Линдисфарна после долгих лет отшельнической жизни на острове Фарн.
Святыня Эдмунда в Бери привлекала паломников со всей Европы.

currentWholeCardLiteral.explanation: Чосер описывает группу паломников, направляющихся в Кентербери к святыне святого Томаса — Томаса Бекета, убитого в 1170 году. Поездка к этой святыне служит рамкой для «Кентерберийских рассказов».

proofs.typedLocator: RPO page, General Prologue headnote prose paragraph beginning “The Canterbury Tales are a series of twenty-four stories”
proofs.quote: The Canterbury Tales are a series of twenty-four stories, supposed to be related by members of a band of pilgrims on their way to the shrine of St. Thomas at Canterbury. A general Prologue and a number of head-links and end-links describe the pilgrims and narrate the effect of the tales and the events of the journey; but there are gaps in the sequence, and the number of stories planned is not completed.
proofs.context: This is the complete relevant headnote paragraph. It names St Thomas at Canterbury as the pilgrims’ destination and immediately explains that the Prologue describes the pilgrims and journey events.

proofs.typedLocator: RPO General Prologue, line 17 explanatory annotation, gloss “martir”
proofs.quote: martir: Thomas A Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, murdered 1170, canonized 1173.
proofs.context: The annotation identifies the martyr in Chaucer’s line 17 and gives his office, death and canonization dates.

proofs.typedLocator: RPO HTML <title> and visible page title/H1
proofs.context: HTML title is “The Canterbury Tales: General Prologue | RPO”; the visible H1 is “The Canterbury Tales: General Prologue”.
Visible masthead identifies the source site.

proofs.typedLocator: Bede, Ecclesiastical History I.VII, full paragraph beginning “This Alban, being yet a pagan”; HTML paragraph 71 (1-based)
proofs.quote: This Alban, being yet a pagan, at the time when the cruelties of wicked princes were raging against Christians, gave entertainment in his house to a certain clergyman, flying from the persecutors. This man he observed to be engaged in continual prayer and watching day and night; when on a sudden the Divine grace shining on him, he began to imitate the example of faith and piety which was set before him, and being gradually instructed by his wholesome admonitions, he cast off the darkness of idolatry, and became a Christian in all sincerity of heart. The aforesaid clergyman having been some days entertained by him, it came to the ears of the wicked prince, that this holy confessor of Christ, whose time of martyrdom had not yet come, was concealed at Alban's house. Whereupon he sent some soldiers to make a strict search after him. When they came to the martyr's house, St. Alban immediately presented himself to the soldiers, instead of his guest and master, in the habit or long coat which he wore, and was led bound before the judge.
proofs.context: Full source paragraph says Alban sheltered the fleeing cleric, observed his prayer, was instructed, and later presented himself in the cleric’s place.

proofs.typedLocator: Bede, Ecclesiastical History IV.XXVII, full first paragraph beginning “THE same year that King Egfrid departed this life”; HTML paragraph 218 (1-based)
proofs.quote: THE same year that King Egfrid departed this life, he (as has been said) promoted to the bishopric of the church of Lindisfarne the holy and venerable Cuthbert, who had for many years led a solitary life, in great continence of body and mind, in a very small island, called Farne, distant almost nine miles from that same church, in the ocean. From his very childhood he had always been inflamed with the desire of a religious life; but he took upon him the habit and name of a monk when he was a young man: he first entered into the monastery of Melrose , which is On the bank of the river Tweed, and was then governed by the Abbot Eata, a meek and simple man, who was afterwards made bishop of the church of Hagulstad or Lindisfarne, as has been said above, over which monastery at that time was placed Boisil, a priest of great virtue and of a prophetic spirit. Cuthbert, humbly submitting himself to this man's direction., from him received both the knowledge of the Holy Scriptures, and example of good works.
proofs.context: The complete paragraph explicitly joins his elevation to Lindisfarne, years of solitary life, the island Farne, and his monastic formation. It is sufficient for every factual element in note2.

proofs.typedLocator:
Abbey of St Edmund Heritage Partnership, full second

, paragraph beginning “Edmund was the King of the East Angles”
proofs.quote: Edmund was the King of the East Angles, until he was killed by the invading Danes in 869. In 903, Edmund’s body was brought to Bury St Edmunds, which was then called Beodricsworth. King Canute founded an Abbey around Edmund’s tomb in 1020 and the shrine of St Edmund attracted pilgrims from all over Europe to visit and to say a prayer.
proofs.context: This full paragraph identifies the Bury location and the shrine’s pilgrims; the next paragraph says visiting pilgrims donated gifts, land and revenues.
